newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB finds small number of unclaimed assets.
newsitem.headline: SNB finds small number of unclaimed assets.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB), cooperating with Swiss banks' overall investigations into activities which may involve claims by Nazi victims, reported Friday it had found only a small number of unclaimed private assets on its own books.

"In the context of current investigations concerning Switzerland's financial relations during the Second World War, the National Bank is conducting extensive research into its archives. These efforts have led to the discovery of only a small number of accounts and safe deposit boxes which were maintained at the SNB and which might be remotely connected with the topical issue of dormant assets," the SNB said.
Assets included three accounts with a total value of 28,000 francs, and a "safekeeping" account which contained a "no longer identifiable number of gold coins."

These assets were reported to the Swiss Federal Office of Justice of the Federal Department of Justice and Police in 1962 under a decree pertaining to disclosure of assets of foreigners suffering racial, religious or political persecution.
In addition there were 15,000 francs on the SNB's own accounts originating from Swiss and foreign customers. Of that amount, roughly 11,000 francs pertained to foreign customers.
The SNB, as a National Bank, held only a small number of private accounts, and the practice ended in the last decade.

Safekeeping of deposits of money and other assets was thus secondary to its activities as a central bank, and it has already had to face criticism that it bought gold from Nazi Germany, or served as a depot for gold Nazis stole from victims or from countries invaded by Hitler's Germany.
Nonethless, the SNB said it was also participating in efforts to try to find assets of Nazi victims which may have been left in Swiss banks during the war.

"The Swiss National Bank regularly checks the lists of inquiries submitted to the ombudsman of the Swiss banks by former customers and their heirs claiming assets. So far, no persons known to the SNB have appeared on these lists," the SNB said in a statement released Friday.
It said the majority of cases pertained to Swiss nationals, or to balances transferred before 1934, so that a connection between the accounts and Nazi persecution was unlikely.
The SNB said that it had done business on a limited basis with private persons up until the start of the 1980s, following authorisation to conduct such business in 1905.
Documents showed two safe deposit boxes dating from the period 1925 to 1945, it added.
"These (boxes) have never been liquidated but do not contain any assets," the SNB said. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
